utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lojo.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you already mentioned several persons that you saw in your room with injuries. Now I would like to know from you, did you see persons returning with injuries from beatings in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw persons who had been beaten and who were returned as such into the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names? Whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Dzanko and Emir Mandzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hasan Dzanko, does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does: Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Emir Mandzo, does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emir? No, I didn't know of any. He was a male nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Hasan Dzanko, who was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a salesperson. He worked in a sales company. He actually had a shop in Josanica, which is a very small place near Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the 13th of June, 1992. That was the third day of the Bajram, the Muslim holiday, the Kurban Bajram. This is a customary procedure. The duty policeman would go to the gate. He would come with a list and call out certain names. On that day, there were five or six persons who were taken to the administration of the KP Dom. On that day, among others, the name of Hasan Dzanko was called out. He was taken to the gate. The duty policeman handed him over to another one. That's where this exchange took place, at the gate. After some time, we heard moans of that person, so it seemed apparent that there was something physical going on with him. And this took place for about 15 minutes, as in most cases. He was taken back to the room again. The guard on duty escorted him through the gate. Whoever dared get close to the window saw that it was difficult for him to walk. When he came to the room, he had injuries on his head, cuts. And also, his chest had been injured, so the physician in our room came to the conclusion that his ribs were broken. This same physician used a needle and thread to sew the wound on his face. After his name, Emir Mandzo's name was called out. He went through the same procedure. Again we heard the moaning. He was also returned after 15 or 20 minutes with a bad limp. Afterwards, he said that both were beaten by Ivanovic. I personally don't know him. His leg was injured and other parts of his body. His leg was hit by a rifle butt. His fingers were broken. He was beaten on the soles of his feet. He was turned over a chair. He described this to us. For some time, we brought meals to him from the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but in the transcript, it doesn't say "neighbour Ivanovic," and that's what the witness said. The witness said "neighbour Ivanovic." It is line 24, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that your numbering must be different. I'd say on page 3, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, my mistake, Your Honour. Yes, page 3, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, perhaps you can clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to clear up Mr. Ivanovic, who that could have been. I come to this a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It might be a good idea to ask him now while it's fresh in everyone's mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about Ivanovic, who that was?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just said -- I mean, both of them confirmed that this same neighbour -- I mean, he's from a neighbouring village, or rather it's the same village but part of the village was Serb and the other part was Muslim, and that that neighbour, when they were brought in by the guards, was the one who did these physical things to them. But let me add one thing. The fact is that this was done within the compound of the prison, according to procedure. That is to say, their names were called out from the gate, and then also the guard came with a written document and called out these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But this neighbour, Ivanovic, neighbour from which village?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Village of Josanica, the Serb part of that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this Ivanovic a guard or someone from outside?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. We did not see him within the compound. What his position was, I don't know. I don't know, at least. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just describing the injuries of Mr. Mandzo. Please continue with that. You said that he had injuries on the feet. What kind of injuries?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A blow in the foot which caused bones to be broken and therefore he could not walk. I already mentioned that. For some time, he had to lie in bed. But he had been beaten all over his body. I'm not aware of these techniques, but he described this to us, that they put him on a chair, over a chair, so that they could beat him on the soles of his feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was he not able to walk? Do you recall how many days?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 days. We would bring him meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dzanko, how long was he not -- how much time did he need to recover?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhat longer because this person was about 70 years old. While he was at the KP Dom, he never actually recovered because the effects of these blows in the chest were really bad and his sleep was affected. Both were taken away in August and there has been no trace of them since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it happened in June. At what time -- at what time of the day did this happen?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime between 10.30 and 12.30 because, in addition to them, there were persons who were taken out from other rooms during that same time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were from other rooms. I knew them but I've forgotten by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Emir Mandzo, that's Schedule B, number 37, and Hasan Dzanko, the Prosecution believes it is B-18, coming from the nickname, although in the list he is listed as Hasan Dzano.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one of the doctors, one of the detainee doctors, helped Mr. Dzanko. Did the two persons you mentioned, did they also get treatment from the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In principle, we tried to help such people with what we had, with compresses made of onions and salt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you heard the sounds of moaning. Did you -- could you find out or could you hear from which direction it came? Could you make out where these persons were beaten?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the sound, it came from the ground floor of the KP Dom. Because of our general psychological condition, people were very afraid and very tense. They were afraid that their names would be called out next, so we suggested to some of them to withdraw from the rooms. It was not a very good idea for anyone to be at the window and to look out of the window. The sound came from the rooms. When one enters the KP Dom on the right-hand side, on the ground floor, one could perhaps see silhouettes in the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you look through the windows? I mean, could you -- what were the window panes like?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the glass was painted white so you could not see through that glass what was going on inside, but perhaps you could discern the silhouette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These sounds -- you said you heard the sounds of moaning. Could you also hear the sounds of beatings, actually the beating as such?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would hear blows, but you didn't know what it was all about until the man would come back to the room. And as I have already mentioned, quite a few of us had withdrawn because if you were to stick around the window, there was an imminent danger of you being the next one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This incident, was it the first time that you heard such sounds of beatings, or was it -- had it happened before and did it happen after that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the first that I had personally heard and actually seen the injured persons afterwards. After that, people were taken out every day in the afternoon, and that went on until the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of the day were the other groups called out?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 30-odd men who were taken out between the 15th and 30th of June, that mainly took place in the afternoon, between 1700 and 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have something like a roll call in your rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was the same. The guard who would be on duty in the compound, he would go to the gate, come back with a piece of paper, and depending on the room involved, he would call out one, two, or three names, and then these men would be taken to the gate. From our room, we could notice through the open gate that they were taken over by another guard and would be searched by that guard then. They didn't take anything with them, but this person would just search their clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they search the clothes; could you see that? Was it in front of the metal door, or where?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. No, after the metal door. If there were two, for example, you would notice that one would get in and then the other one, and you would notice that this guard who was taking them in at the door would search them briefly, and then they would be taken to the premises of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was actually referring to another sort of roll call. Were you checked on every evening or every day in the room as such, all detainees?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure of work of this institution, this camp, was to a large extent based on the procedure that prevailed in civilian times when the KP Dom was an official institution. Every evening, the duty guard would come, accompanied by a guard from the compound. They had automatic weapons. They would enter the rooms. This would usually be after dinner. We would all line up, one behind the other, in the joint premises so that it would be easier to see how many of us there were. One of us would be appointed the person in charge of that room, sort of, and then that one person would tell these guards who had came in how many of us there actually were, and perhaps he would say whether somebody had been taken out that day. Those who could not get to that joint room, that common room, like Dzanko and others, we would say that they had stayed behind in bed. They would record that in their notebooks which they carried with them, because they were going from one room to the other that way. That was the procedure that prevailed throughout my stay at the KP Dom. So they had the exact situation every evening, how many persons there were in the KP Dom, or rather, the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say after dinner, what time of the day was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes around 7 or 7.30 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this procedure that you just explained to us, several detainees were singled out and taken to the metal door, when did this take place; after this roll call or before, or both?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before and after the roll call. So we would always correct the actual figure. We would always say exactly how many of us were in the room, but I already mentioned that people were usually taken out between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. five and nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any names of such detainees that were called out, waited in front of the metal door, and that you heard --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I wrote down the names I could remember, and that is annexed to those documents of mine. May I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Munib Veiz, Marinovic Kruno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let's -- whenever you mention a name, let's just deal with this person, and when we are finished, then we go to the next. Munib Veiz, what can you tell us about him; who he was, what happened to him, what you saw or heard?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munib Veiz was a salesperson in Foca. He worked in the shoe shop of the big leather factory, Visoko, from Visoko. My assumption is that he was taken away and beaten up because every individual or every two individuals who were taken out, after they were taken out and after they passed the gate, we would hear moans after some time, that is to say that they underwent physical treatment, all of those who had passed that gate, including Munib Veiz. Also, I think that because of something that happened before the war, Munib Veiz was the friend of Murid, the director of Focatrans, and that is one of the reasons why such force was applied against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Veiz, Munib Veiz, again?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not him, not anyone else from these groups that were taken out later. 25

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Munib Veiz is listed under B-59 and C-28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go to the next person from your list and tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kruno Marinovic was a Croat who came to Foca. As far as I know, he was a mechanic that maintained various appliances in Foca, and also he was a correspondent from time to time for some Croat newspaper, I don't know which one exactly. I don't know the exact dates when each one of them was taken out, and -- but it is definitely this period between the 15th and 30th, and he went through the same procedure as Veiz did, and I don't know anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is number C-15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, the next person?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mato Ivancic, he was a medical technician. He worked in the regional medical centre. He was not in the same room with me, but as far as I know, he was brought from his workplace, from the hospital, and also taken away according to the same procedure as the previous person. He was mistreated. Another observation: His documents, his passport, that is, we found in Room 21, and that was left behind him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour it's C-11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, the next name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic is a youngish man. I did not know him that well, so there is not much I can say, but his fate was the same as that of the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's C-26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic was assistant commander of the police in Foca before the war, and to the best of my knowledge, at the KP Dom, he was physically mistreated twice, once before I came to the KP Dom and the second time in this period between the 15th and the 30th, when he was taken away. Again, he was beaten and he never returned, and I don't know anything about him, just like the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this person Nurko Nisic, that's C-19 and the incident 5.27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halim Konjo, who was one of Konjo brothers, and they were in the KP Dom. He owned a restaurant at Gornje Polje, and he was a person well-known in Foca, very sociable, and people knew his pub through his father and otherwise, and he had friends among all the ethnic groups. He was quite relaxed and behaved very freely so that people around the town knew him. And he was taken away following the same procedure, and when it was him -- because others who were more characteristic, for instance, we observed that he was ill-treated the longest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is C-13 and B-33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Selimovic, the same procedure. I think he was a car mechanic and had his own shop, as far as I know. And it was following the same procedure, that he was called out, left, and is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the first name of Mr. Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know his nickname, and they called him Spona.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that it is B-50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz likewise. I know him but not all that well. But it was the same procedure; again, he was taken away and he fared the same way as others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is C-29, and this Zulfo Veiz is also mentioned under 5.27 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, doesn't quite ring the bell, but I do think that he was a policeman, as far as I can remember, but I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two Veiz, are they relatives, Munib and Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuad Mandzo was a youngish person of some 25. I believe that he came out of a vocational school. He lived in Donje Polje and he is missing too, like those others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramo Dzendusic. He was of a rather advanced age, 65 or thereabouts. He was a clerk in the municipal authorities. That is, he worked for the Secretariat for National Defence, which was responsible for the draft in the former JNA, so that everybody knew that person rather well. He lived in Donje Polje. And about him, I know the day, the date and the time when he was taken away, the hour when he was taken away. And it was the 30th of June, 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this date so well? Is there a particular reason to remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stuck in my memory because nobody else was taken after that and because we were sitting in the same room when the man on duty came and called him out, so that simply that day and the time when he was taken away simply stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, the next person?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nail Hodzic, he was a taxi driver, although relatively advanced age, in Foca. Practically everybody in Foca knew him, and he was taken away, like all the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's B-10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bico, he was also a publican. He had his restaurant in Gornje Polje. He was taken away. He was a well-known figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his first name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bico owned a restaurant, a coffee shop, the name I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's C-2 and this person is also mentioned under B-5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Kuloglija was a teacher. I believe he worked in the elementary school at Ustikolina beyond that part of the town which was called Aladza, and he was taken away following the same procedure and he is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's C-15 (Couldn't hear).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Granov, an engineer, the first name I do not recall. He worked for -- he was employed with the local post office, and I think he came from the part of the town called Gornje Polje. He was taken away and is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that it is C-9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atko Isanovic, a young man who was also taken away. I do not have any particular information about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person is mentioned under B-29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Altoka, I know his last name, a local worker, as far as I know. He was taken away, and I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that this is the person C-1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, continue.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esad Kiselica. He was employed with the electric -- with the power distribution board in Foca, and he was employed with the unit maintaining the low voltage network in Foca. And he was taken away like all the others, and again, like all the others, I do not know what happened to him. He is missing. Those are the ones that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is C-12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the brothers Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew them, but now it's difficult for me to remember their faces, their traits, after all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only ask you because in your notes, in the notes that you referred to, you have listed names of people that were taken away, and there is the name Rikalo, but no first name. That's why I ask.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've forgotten quite a lot by now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person Mensud Pasovic? You have listed him as well in your notes.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pasovic. One of Pasovic brothers, if you mean him, but they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. taken away later. They were -- or one of them was with that group which allegedly went to pick plums, and another brother was with that group which went to Rozaje, and he is alive. I mean, he let us know that he was alive. And about this one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an Abdurahman Cankusic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surname rings a bell, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Kemo Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he -- what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemo Dzelilovic was a teacher at, I believe, the secondary vocational school. And he was also with that group which was taken away, and he went through the same procedure, and I know nothing else about him. I don't know if he ever called from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is C-7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a Seval Soro?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seval, it also rings a bell, but I've forgotten what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you heard the sound of moaning and the sound of beating. Did you hear anything else in relation to these beatings and the disappearance of these people you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several cases, as I've told you, such as Halim Konjo, Munib Veiz, and Nurko Niksic, I can still -- somehow I can hear still in my ears is that they were tortured for the longest periods of time. In Konjo's case in particular, one could hear voices as when somebody falls because he has fainted and then somebody's trying to bring him back to consciousness by pouring water over him, calling out his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever recognise the voice of those who beat? Could you tell us who beat these people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I couldn't recognise -- no, I couldn't identify the voice of the one who beat, to identify him, no. But according to those in the room, those who knew guards or the personnel of the KP Dom better than I did, they -- most the name -- among them the name "Burilo" came up most frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Burilo, is that -- was that a guard?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the war and wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Mr. Rasevic about these, these disappearances and these beatings?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning in June, on two or three occasions I received some information about my family from Mr. Rasevic, and I asked him, "And where are those that are been taken away? What's happened with them, because they don't seem to be coming back?" And he told me that they had been taken to another place. As far as I can remember, he said that they had been taken to Velecevo, which was the women's prison before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Rasevic from before the war? Were you friendly with each other?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rasevic and I grew up together in the same street, and we attended the elementary school together. We were in the same classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pattern of beatings in June, how did this affect you? Did you fear to be taken as well?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was afraid. There was no exception because nobody knew the criteria for which they were calling you out, so any one of us could have been the one. There was this fear, the suspense, because we never knew who would be the next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself had a rather high position in Foca before the war. Do you know why -- what saved you from being taken? Did you think about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think about it until I came out of the KP Dom because I didn't know how long it would last. And even because of this situation, since we knew nothing about those who had been taken away since isolation and secrecy were such that we could have absolutely no, no way to know that those people who had gone out had not reached their homes, that is, their families. I must say that during those months when they were being taken away, we -- privately we were all glad when they came and called names out, and we were sorry that we were not with those groups, that we were staying behind, so that we thought, and I thought about myself, that we were being kept there longer for some other reasons because they perhaps needed us for something or other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, let me interrupt you. I was not asking you about the exchanges. I was asking you about these beatings, when the people disappeared in the beatings. Do you know why you were not, why you yourself were not taken out in this fashion, beating and disappearance? That was what I was having at. Did someone help you or save you, or what saved you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not know, that I began to think about it only later on. I suppose that before the war, as I held all those offices, and I suppose I treated people in the town in a manner that somebody appreciated, really, and therefore they did not put me on such a list. I simply do not have the real answer. I suppose those who decided who would be put on the list and who wouldn't would know best why that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already started to talk about exchanges, and you said that you actually wanted to be exchanged. What kind -- what did you find out later about these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acquired that knowledge when I reached Samobor, that all those who left, that is over 400 men, I believe, that most of them were not exchanged, that is, were not set free, but were simply gone, and all trace of their physical existence is gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have listed in your notes a lot of these exchanges, and you have also counted who was later heard of and never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to enter this document now into evidence, that is, the document ID 215 and 215A, so that we do not have to name here each and every person on this list. I would only speak with the witness about these incidents as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But so far he has simply boldly asserted in a general sense that they have not been heard of again. Is that sufficient? Shouldn't we have some idea of his opportunity to know those facts? If you remember the way the investigator went about it, he made inquiries of people who would be expected to know. Some witnesses, during the course of the trial, have said that when they were released, they were bombarded by inquiries from the families of these people as to whether he knew anything about it, which suggests that they knew nothing about it. But so far, we don't seem to have got any evidentiary basis for using his list to prove that they are no longer in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have listed about, I don't know, about 20 or even more exchanges, and you have listed the people that were exchanged on what day, and the number of people. How do you know -- how did you learn that these people are actually missing? What did you do to find out? Whom did you meet so that you can be sure about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the accuracy of my information, about many of them, I heard from families who communicated with me from different European countries, having learned that I had come out. And in May, the Club of Fortunes in Germany invited me. They organised a meeting, and at this meeting, which brought together members of families of a large number of those men, and I told them, because they asked me were they there, did I see them there and when did they come out? And I gave them dates then and they confirmed that it was about that time when they came out that they never called them until the time when I came out. I also said yesterday that I had been to the International Red Cross in Zagreb and spoke to the person who kept lists of registered Foca locals who were missing, so that there I also learnt about the names of the missing persons, that is, that they had never called anyone, communicated either with the International Red Cross somewhere in Bosnia or any other part of the world because, according to the computer evidence of the Red Cross, they had all this information, where the person had called from, whom he had called home from, and whom he'd called where, and what camp he had been detained in. And the International Red Cross, I could see that on their computer, had a list of all camps in Bosnia and the names of those which were missing. When I look at those lists at the International Red Cross, I could not find out if they had possibly been transferred to some other camps, and it was impossible that they had been taken from Foca to another camp. If there were such cases, and in 1993, I had some information to that effect, namely that from Foca, from the KP Dom, in June, 1993, a group of men had been taken to Rudo, of those 81 who were still left behind, and the Red Cross recorded that duly. About two, they were, for instance, put on record in Butmir. So that there was an absolute control. And these men are de facto missing to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now we are getting closer, but if you want us to make findings, either we do it witness by witness in that list, or you have to get something from the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- which will satisfy us that each of those names is covered by those various matters. The inquiries that have been made by this witness are the same sort of inquiries as have been made by the investigator, but he has been able to say in his lists that he's made them in relation to precisely-named people. So if you want us to make a finding that those particular people are no longer to be found, I'm afraid you'd have to take the witness through bit by bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will take him through these exchanges he's listed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But certainly the sorts of inquiries he has made are the very sort of inquiries that would establish that fact, provided we can pin them to each particular name on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have listed in your notes -- you have listed an incident from 15th August, 1992, and you have written here that 15 men were taken. What can you tell us about this group of 15 men? And you have listed here Zaim, the manager of the post office, Dzanko brothers and Kibrici brothers. What did you find out -- what did you personally observe while you were in the prison and what did you find out later about these people you have mentioned by name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 19th of August, not the 15th. These individuals whom I mentioned were by and large in the same room as I was. Rasid Pacanic, Paco were father and son. Lagariya, one of the twin brothers from the village of Kosman, they were with their father in the camp. Zaim Cedic. Mulahasanovic, Fehim Mulahasanovic, an old man that is over 70, from Miljevina. And Zaim and his son. About some of those, I know precisely, at the request of the families, such as the old Mulahasanovices, I know that he never called them, that he is still missing and still trying to trace him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About which of these persons do you know that, those you just --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mulahasanovic, Fehim Mulahasanovic, Zaim Cedic, and father and son Paco because the other Paco was taken away on the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what can you tell us about the group that was taken away on the 22nd of August? How many were they and what did you later hear about them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a group of about 17 men. I mentioned Ismet Paco first. He was one of the directors in Focatrans. He was a deputy director in Focatrans, or rather he was director of freight transportation. And Focatrans is well-known because of the events that took place before the war. Tatarevic Nedim, a young man with degree in economics, he worked in the bank. He was director of the treasury of the foreign exchange sector. He was taken away just like Smajkan Sacir. Until the present day, their families know nothing of them. I know about them for sure, that they are missing until the present day. As for the rest I've mentioned, the same goes for them as well, except that I haven't been in touch with their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you know -- how do you know that the others are also missing? Where did you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From people who got out of the camp in 1993, through this mutual exchange of information, Bibovic Ismet, Ekrem Selimovic, confirmed that these people were still missing and that they also, through their information, through their families, they came to the conclusion that they had not contacted them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the group -- you have listed also a group of 25 people who were taken away on the 25th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this group was also my wife's brother, who has not been heard from since. That is something I know for sure. Lojo Nedzib is my relative. His wife was in Zagreb for some time. He's never called either. Pasovic Ismet was brought from Montenegro, from Igalo. He is an elderly man also, a close friend. He never called. He's never been heard from. Asim Nezbur, a photographer, his wife lives in Sarajevo. He's never been heard from since. Jakupovic Safet, before the war -- I mean, he's not from Foca. He was a convict in the KP Dom, and when he was released from prison, he got married to a woman in Foca. He has never been heard from. I know from his brothers-in-law, his wife's brothers, that he's never been heard from since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your notes, you have mentioned a group of 71 detainees that were taken away on the 29th of August, 1992. What happened on that 29th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of August, I don't know whether that was one of the results of the London conference and its conclusions. We heard about that, that all camps in Bosnia were supposed to be closed down and that there was supposed to be an exchange all for all. People were being taken out more intensively. And on that Saturday, first a group of 55 men was taken out to Rozaje, and in the afternoon, as I said here, these men were taken in three groups. This went on for almost two hours. Mr. Rasevic would come from the gate with a list and he would call out people's names in different rooms, telling them to take their belongings and to get ready. And then the guards would come and take them to the gate where they were all grouped, and then they would go out, one by one or two by two, and then probably because they had to be searched, they would get out through the gate slower. As one group would leave, then another list would be brought and then they would leave in the same way, and then the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. list for the third group came. So at one moment I asked Rasevic at the door when he was calling out people's names, I said, "Has the moment come for us all to go?" And he said, "I don't know, I'm very busy. This is going on now." So we thought with this group of 55, that indeed the decisions of the London conference were being implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have listed -- among these people who were taken out, you have listed Hasan Dzano and Emir Mandzo. Are these the two that you have told us about who were beaten up in your room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, what did you hear about these people who were taken on that day? Are they missing? Did they survive? Did they show up?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also through their families, I know that absolutely no one from these groups has been heard from since then, except for the people who I mentioned, those who had taken the bus. The 55 who were taken away and who were supposed to be exchanged through Montenegro, their names were called out in the morning. They got ready. They were in a room next to the restaurant because they were waiting for the bus. They boarded the bus. They left. However, in the early evening, the entire group reappeared all of a sudden at the KP Dom. These 55 persons were split up because 32 -- actually, that same day when that group of 71 had been called out, that night when they were taken away, 23 were put into a room next to us, but that was in a different wing of the building. I think this was Room 13, where they spent the entire night. And we found out from them that Pero Elez had returned them. He was a Vojvoda in the Serb hierarchy. Just before Niksic, he said, "Everyone goes back." These 23 were taken by bus again on the next day, and when I got out of the camp, I found out that they were then taken to Rozaje, actually. These names are included in that group, all of them, and they all contacted their families. They're all alive today except for Hamdija Hadzimuratovic who's died in the meantime. He was a heart patient anyway, and he passed away in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned the 71 detainees that were taken on that same day, and you have listed Hasan Dzano, Emir Mandzo, and Sanin Kulelija. Did you get information that any of these 71 survived, be it later on?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish that were true, but not a single one has been heard from. Actually, they're missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have listed an exchange for the 10th September 1992, and you have listed there 41 detainees were taken on that day.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about their fate?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among them is this group Divjan, Fadil; Kafedzic, Edhem; Hadzimesic, Meho; Semso Cankusic; Reko. That is the son of the hodza who was well-known as a kind of witch doctor, too. In that group was this young one, Rahman. He was the youngest of all. His father worked in my mine. This Rahman was the youngest; he was 15. None of them has been heard since then. Fadil Divjan and I said good-bye to each other and - how should I put this? - he lent me 50 Deutschemarks. None of them has contacted my family or me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the group that you have listed, 50 detainees were taken on the 12th September 1992, what can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a period when people were taken out very intensively. I mean "intensively," every week something was going on. So we were all convinced that during the month of September we would all be exchanged, so we didn't pay that much attention to it anymore because we thought that our detention was just about over, and we were all hoping that we would see each other somewhere else. Nezbur is there, too, who is the brother of Asim, the photographer. I know about him for sure, that he's been missing. I mean, he's never been heard from since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have listed under 17 September 1992, you listed groups -- two groups that were called out for picking plums. Can you tell us what happened on the 17th of September?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, the guard on duty came again, and first he asked for a sort of work group to volunteer, and a number of people volunteered. And there were some of us who also said, Well, yes, take us if this is some kind of action, because we all wanted to get out, really. If you would go out like that, then you would get bigger meals, too. However, nevertheless, he came with a list and called out certain persons' names. He did not accept any volunteers, although people had volunteered. So in that group -- I mean, before lunch a group was called out. This was around 20 past 10, and they were all in my room for the most part, those whose names were called out, that is to say, Hajro Klinac, Edib Muminovic. Then this Dzano, Ramiz, the taxi driver from Ustikolina. Halid Konjo, the brother of the previously-mentioned Konjo. He is one of the persons whose corpses were identified because last year a commission found the corpses of these seven persons from that group. As for Halid Konjo, his mortal remains were buried in Sarajevo last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other persons that you -- are listed here and named in regard of this group, did you hear of them again? Did you have contact with their relatives, and do you know if they are still missing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they are still registered as missing because another one of my wife's brothers, Mirsad Hadzimesic, is among them, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have listed a group for that same day of plum pickers that were taken out later that day.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just to digress a bit; as for this plum picking, I heard about that from the guard in the camp because we expected these men to come back the same night. Since they did not come back that night, on next day others asked me to ask, and I did ask Vlatko Pljevaljcic, a guard in the camp, what was going on with these people; what was going on with them? And he said, "Don't worry, they'll come back after they pick plums. They're picking plums." So that's where this term comes from, "plum picking."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they come back?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have listed in your notes five names, Mirsad Hadzimesic, Murat Crneta, Dzemo Balic, Gordan Hukovic, and Nermin Pasovic. Did you inquire about their fate, and what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pasovic, Nermin, his father recently died in Sarajevo. I know that his son never called again. Balic, Dzemo, his brothers are in Sarajevo. I talked to them. He's never returned. Crneta, Murat, an engineer, he worked in Maglic. He was one of the directors. His wife Zineta, with a degree in economics, worked at the SDK. That's a financial institution in the former system. He's never been heard of since. And then my brother-in-law, Mirsad Hadzimesic. And I don't know about Sulejman, I haven't heard from his family, but I imagine that he's never been heard of since as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have listed also an exchange for 11th of December, 1992. What can you tell us about this exchange?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a group that was brought in, or rather, singled out of the rooms, from Room 16. And this eighth person, I don't know his name, he was taken from Room 18 and also from our room. Fahrudin Malkic worked at the Ones [phoen] factory. He was a school mate of mine, an acquaintance of mine. He's never been heard of. Aziz Sahinovic, a distant relative of my wife's. His wife was a director of the bank in Foca. She works in Sarajevo today. She's there with her daughters. They've never heard from their father. Ekrem Cengic, he is the brother of another Cengic who worked in the National Defence Department in Foca. He's never been heard of. Halim Dedovic, the barber I talked about. Ibrahim Kafedzic, I assume the same thing, but I haven't had any contact with his close relatives. Also as for these, Lagarija, the father of those twins who had been taken away before. And this Slovenian journalist, Alojz Krivograd, who was brought in from an isolation cell, I heard of his details in Samobor, in Zagreb. His family expressed interest, and also journalists from his newspaper got in contact with me and asked me whether I knew anything about him. However, I could not say anything to them, and I told them to get in touch with the Red Cross and others because they had not heard from him until the time when I was making these lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in relation to the people you just mentioned, they are missing, and you heard it from their relatives or the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have listed an incident on 16 January 1993 referring to three from the Cengic family. What can you tell us about this incident? What happened? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three persons were together in the same room, in Room 21. Actually, we found them there when we were brought there in December, from 18 to 16, that is. They were in that room and with them was another man, (redacted), who was brought in from the hospital. On that day or, rather, the day before that because they were taken away on the 16th, the guard came and called out all of their three names, but he said that he -- they should come but not take anything with them, that they should go to see the warden at the administrative building. Fehim Cengic, I mentioned that here, he was a blind person. He was aged over 60; Hilmo Cengic was in his 50s, he worked for me at the mine as a guard; and Muhamed Cengic who was over 80 years old. When they returned, then Hilmo told me that at the warden, at warden's office they found a high-ranking military officer who questioned them, what kind of relations they had, et cetera, because an intervention had come from very high places, from Milosevic personally, that they should be exchanged, because their brother Fahrudin Cengic, who worked in Sarajevo before the war, was the director of Autobosna, and he was in a pretty high position. He was a personal friend of Slobodan Milosevic's, and through him he intervened so that his brothers could be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information, did you hear it from the three Cengices, or you said Hilmo Cengic, or what you just told us, did you hear that from Hilmo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Hilmo mention if the warden was present when they talked to this high-ranking military person?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He mentioned that the warden was in the office and that one of the commanders was there. I don't know, that's what he said, but I don't know who was this commander in Foca at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Hilmo mention the warden, or did he actually mention the name of the warden? Do you recall how he spoke about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that conversation he just mentioned the warden. In such conversations, we did not go into any kind of details; we would just said "the warden." It was not that his name was mentioned. He concentrated, actually, on the officer who was questioning him and who probably asked him in greater detail about how come Slobodan Milosevic knew about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who this military officer was? Did Hilmo mention his name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We can only make assumptions. Later on, I found out that two colonels from the JNA were brought to high-ranking military positions in Foca, Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Bozevic. I personally do not know them, though, and I did not know them before the war either, but they are people whose family origins are from the Foca area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have exhausted the list and I would now again like to enter this into evidence. The Defence counsel have seen, meanwhile, the originals, but we would like to enter the copies into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that I do not insist. However, my learned colleague said that we've seen the originals. We have seen the original of this other document that was written in hand, but this other document we saw only in photocopied form. However, we do not object. We do not object to its being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not altogether certain which is the document that you have not seen the original of.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution does only have the original of the printed document that the witness wrote in printed letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do -- our original, so to speak, is also a copy and can you -- maybe Mr. Lojo can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The original of your first notes, did you maybe send them somewhere? Because you did not provide the originals to us, to the Prosecutor. What did you do with the originals of your first notes; do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you recall?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I gave the first original to a journalist who used this for writing an article when I was in Samobor, and this other one is basically the first one rewritten, except with some additional explanations and things like that. So I consider the second one to be an authentic document, a source document, that I relied on the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that having been cleared up, you have no other objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said, Your Honour, that I do not object. I just wanted to be clear, because we heard it being said that we had seen the originals. We had not seen the originals but we do not object to the photocopies being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, they will be Exhibits P215 and P215A. Should they be under seal? Are there any names there that are protected?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There are a few names of witnesses among those exchange -- names of the exchanged people, protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They are?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They will both be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, while were you in the KP Dom, did you have to work in the prison?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there actually a group of people who worked, a permanent group of people who worked?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first, this work was carried out in the following way. Before that, on two or three occasions, lists were compiled in July and August of all the detainees; name, surname, occupation, date of birth or rather year of birth. And probably in order to meet the needs of the KP Dom, individually persons were taken out of various rooms, persons who had different specialities -- masons, mechanics, electricians, carpenters, painters -- probably people who were needed to do something at the KP Dom. Later on, the administration realised that that is how external information reached the rooms directly, so then they actually concentrated all these people who went out to work in one room only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not need to go into the details because we have other witnesses who were actually in this group, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are also running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Lojo, before the break, we briefly touched on the issue of work in the prison, and I would only like to discuss two aspects of this. First of all, was work voluntary, or were the detainees forced to work?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, we can say in a manner of speaking that there was no coercion. People were happy to join the work teams for the simple reason that it enabled them to get a better meal, more food, and thus, they were not threatened by starvation. And secondly, they were not confined to a very small space, being only with the group, because you must know that we were never allowed to leave our rooms for a second. And if you went out to work, it meant going out. It meant some physical exercise, and it meant being in the open air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the detainees have to work on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any such knowledge, with exception of one group of four or five of them, I don't know exactly. One of them was Uzeir Alic, Mehmedalija Lojo from my room. They were taken sometime in September, and they told me afterwards when they returned that they had been taken to military positions facing Gorazde, and that they had been employed to make dugouts. That was a part of preparations for the fortification of lines for the forthcoming winter, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they have to do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did it, as I told you, in September and October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did they have to do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One group went and they were absent for about 20 days from the KP Dom, that is, they spent that time at the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you about the conditions in which they stayed there? Did they actually stay there overnight?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, they spent all their time there. I mean, they slept there. As for the conditions, from what they told me, they were not physically ill-treated. Perhaps somebody abused them verbally, but they were protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was wondering, did they tell you how they slept? Did they have tents, or did they have to sleep in the open, if they talked about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not go into those details. What we wanted to know basically was the fact that they had been taken away, we did not know where, and that they came back, that is, that they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did detainees work in the Miljevina mine while you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While I was there, nobody worked in the mine, except for one individual who worked in Miljevina and in the mine now and then, and that was a car mechanic, Hamdo Hadzic, and he stayed in the police station. And before me, that is, before I came to the KP Dom, according to statements of people in the camp who shared my room, and among them there were also some workers of mine, in May a large group of some 20 men was returned from the KP Dom. They were all former workers of the Miljevina mine who had begun to work in the mine for a short time sometime in May - I learnt about that from their families subsequently - but then for the reason that I do not know, the Serb authorities, rather the mine management, cut short their work there, and they were to be brought back to the camp. That is what they had been told. But they were never brought back to the camp and there are no further news about them. And after I left the camp, reportedly, people from the camp went to the mine and worked, but that was in 1993 and that was after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the KP Dom, did you ever meet journalists and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once, in August, and it was after the 18th, after the London conference. A group of three or four journalists came, and from what I know, one of them was a journalist of Ekspres Politika, at least that's what he -- the paper that he told us he came from. He was escorted by a soldier -- by a guard, excuse me, and Mr. Rasevic, and in the anteroom, in our anteroom, in front of the lavatory and the WC, we gathered around those journalists, a large group of us who were in that room, and they asked us, one of the first questions was: What did we have to say as prisoners of war about a statement by Mr. Izetbegovic about -- and they mentioned a position that then 25, 40, something about that camp; that is, how did he rank the camp in Foca? And I reacted to what he said, that we were prisoners of war, and I said that from -- to the best of my knowledge, none of us had been brought from the front line, that we were all civilians, down to the last one, and I indicated this boy Rahman, who was 15, Hamdija Hadzimuratovic, who had a heart condition, had arrived from the hospital, myself, and I said, "This one comes from the hospital, that one from the street, that one from his flat, and others were brought from their workplaces, like my brother-in-law from the health centre." And I said we were brought only because we were members of a non-Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did these journalists react to that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, we did not talk long because there were others -- no. He said nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these journalists, were they Serbs, from Serbia or were they -- where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically journalists, as far as I could see, they were not foreigners, whether they came from Serbia or Montenegro, that is that part which was covered by all -- from the part which was controlled by the SDS, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell them about the bad conditions and about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never asked us that, and I don't think it was very advisable to talk about that. But they could see from how we looked, they could learn enough about that. They didn't have to ask anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you think it was not advisable to mention it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, I mentioned a name, Alija from Gorazde, a salesman, now his surname comes back to me, it's Cardaklija. He was brought, as I said, from Montenegro, and he was very -- he was shocked by the conditions and everything. He was very afraid, and then he wrote a letter to the warden, encouraged by -- or, rather, that's what the guards recommended to him. He wrote to the warden. I guess he wrote it to him. I did not read it but I saw that he put his requests on two or three sheets of paper. And after he handed over his request, he was called for interview -- for an interview, and I do not know his fate afterwards. So that I don't think any complaints would have been of any help to us; quite the reverse. I think that if you asked for something, if you had some requests, you could only run into trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these the only journalists that you -- that ever came to the KP Dom while you were there? Or did you meet any other?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't know if it was an American or an English team, a lady and the technicians, I mean, cameramen. It was sometime in June, as far as I can remember, the latter half, or perhaps early July. I can't remember the exact date. As far as I know, they did not enter our rooms. They did their recording outside, that is prisoners who were outside and those who were at the windows. And at some point, this lady journalist came to us because we were in Room 16, which is on the ground floor, and she was beckoned by the prisoners and she came closer, and Mr. Medim Tatarevac, who spoke English, and he said a few words to her, that we were not there of our own free will and that we had not been captured in the battlefield, and could she help us to have us released from there? Many of them also asked for cigarettes because, you know -- I mean, when you smoke, you cannot resist. And that was the only communication with them. And that team did not stay there long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the pre-war warden of the KP Dom? Before the war, who was the warden?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden of the civilian part before the war broke out was Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the warden during the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, the commander of the camp was Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the testimony you mentioned that Muslim managers were replaced by Serbs, but wasn't Mr. Tesovic a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojica Tesovic, yes, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know about Mr. Tesovic, he was a highly-accomplished, a highly-educated man, and he was quite an expert in criminal sanctions, and from this I inferred that he did not -- he was rather reluctant to take over that function because he was not a person who would do such things or -- we were personal friends. He was all for education. He applied adult education and rehabilitation measures in the KP Dom Foca, and Foca enjoyed the reputation of one of the most civilised prisons, penitentiaries, in the former Yugoslavia. So I simply think he could not accept to run something like that, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Krnojelac from before the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Krnojelac in 1978 at that time when I was the secretary of the municipal committee. It was the highest party post in the then system. And in addition to the mayor of the municipality, I was the second man. I mean, we held the most important posts in the municipality. And at the time when I was the secretary of the committee, I was, ex officio, head of the committee for all national defence and civil protection. It was a body in the then Yugoslavia which existed in all the municipalities in case of crisis, to deal with crisis. And all of the leading executives in the municipality would sit on that body, I mean, both the business managers and administrative leaders, and at times other people would be drawn in. At that time, Mr. Krnojelac was the commander of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the commander of the reserve force. Was he the highest local person in the military forces? What does it mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The witness did not say "the commander." He said "the president," and then said reserve officer, and I think it was a slip rather than that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. The transcript records him as having said, was "the commander" of the reserve force. Now, if the transcript is right, then the question was appropriate. Are you saying that the answer was wrongly recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The witness said that he was the president, and I think he even stopped, and I believe it was a slip of the tongue, and then he said he was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not -- just one moment. We're not interested in slips of the tongue. What we are concerned with is what the witness said. Now, if you say that it has been wrongly translated or wrongly recorded in the transcript, we'll listen to you; but I'm not going to change something because it was, as you say, a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript, Your Honours. He did not say "commander"; he said "president."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. We'll get it cleared up, then. I think you'd better ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the exact position of Mr. Krnojelac at that time? What was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the reserve force of the association of reserve officers, and that existed in all the municipalities of Yugoslavia. So he was not the commander. That is not a military formation of any kind. It is an association -- you asked me how did I know Mr. Krnojelac, so my first -- our first contacts date back to that period, and that is long before the war. It's 1978, 1979. It's an association which brings together all those who had served the army but were not active officers. They were all members of that association. They were officers from lieutenant to captains onwards, and in that association they heard lectures about new military doctrines, new weapons, and so on and so forth from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krnojelac, did he have a military rank, and would you know which?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have a rank; I don't know which. I mean, I just don't remember whether he was a lieutenant, a captain, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he was the president of this association of reserve officers. During which time period?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said while I was the secretary of the committee, so it was 1978, 1979, 1980, within that segment of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he stopped being the president of this association?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they had terms of office there, and I think -- I don't really know the statute of that association, but when Tito died in 1981, this system of collective leadership was introduced with people rotating in the leading posts, and that also covered the association. So all of these posts, all these functions, I think, were for one-year periods of time, that is, a term of office was one year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krnojelac continue to be a reserve officer after 1980, 1981, as you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, always. It was a lasting obligation as long as one was a potential conscript. Under that system, nobody could be relieved of the military obligation until the age of 70, except that one could be either active duty or a member of the reserve force, that is, in the Territorial Defence, or one could be assigned for a wartime labour duty if that went with his function, but one could not be relieved of it. One could not stop being a member of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned the age, when you reach a certain age you are automatically out of this obligation. Are there other possibilities to get out of this obligation to be in the reserve forces when you were an officer?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in case of an illness, illness that would be such that would preclude one from serving his military duty. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when the war began and conflicts in Foca, we learnt on various occasions who was on the other side and who was doing what on that side, because to begin with, one could still move around the town still, one still communicated. And the first people to be taken away, including my wife's brother, he was taken away as early as the 9th of April from the health centre to -- he was taken to Livade with another group of health workers from the health centre. And after that when the Muslim population withdrew from Donje Polje and where the KP Dom was converted into a camp, they were all transferred from Livade and others were brought into custody, including my other brother-in-law. And during those first ten days, families were allowed to visit the prisoners in the camp, and my wife and her mother went there to visit them. And on that occasion, she learned from my brothers-in-law who ran the camp, that is, about Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, did you ever speak with him while you were detained, with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the prison staff members mention to you that Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
