utterances.text: Once. I said that I was -- that Mr. Rasevic and I knew one another, and in passing I asked him about Mr. Tesovic, what happened to him. And he mentioned Mr. Krnojelac as a warden, and said that Mr. Tesovic was temporarily at Velecevo at the KP Dom's farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have this conversation?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the month of June, because he conveyed a message to me that my family was still in Foca and that they were well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk with Mr. Rasevic on this occasion or on other occasions about anything else in relation to KP Dom and how it was functioning?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was some kind of secrecy involved. I think that the staff of the KP Dom was kind of afraid of any kind of longer contact, so any conversation would be two or three sentences only. With Mr. Rasevic, I would talk only in passing, when he would come to our room. So you couldn't ask him in the compound or somewhere else, only if he would enter the room and talk to us. I know that once in July, he said to me that some of my Serb friends were working on my release. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the accused -- did you see Mr. Krnojelac in the prison?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Krnojelac a few times as he was passing from the gate towards the canteen, towards where the laundry was, the kitchen. I don't know what was being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing when you saw him? Was he just walking?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw was that he was just walking. I don't know whether he was escorted by one person or two. Once I saw him on his own but, as a rule, he always had someone with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who? Who was this other person or these other persons who were with him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Staff from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Krnojelac wearing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see a weapon on him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether he carried a pistol or not, I could not say with 100 per cent certainty. Usually when the metal gate would close, you would hear it, and from 16 we would look out and we would usually comment on who this was, but if this person was not going towards us, it was not really something that we would particularly register.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the second in command, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who the second in command was because we did not see a list on which we would see that this was the second in command or were we ever told, "This is your commander, this is the second in command." It is on the basis of how duties were carried out that we came to the conclusion that Mr. Savo Todovic was the second in command, and that Mr. Rasevic, because he did not do guard duty, was a commander or something else, and Mr. Gagovic, who came later, was also part of the top echelon of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis of facts did you conclude that Mr. Savo Todovic was the second in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was the one who did the organising. We thought that he was the one who was in charge of work duties. In principle, he was the one who would assign people to go to work. Often he would come and carry out individual conversations. I mean, in the guards' premises, he would call people in for an interview, according to some criterion of his own -- we didn't realise what that was -- so that he would find out some pieces of information, whatever. He would talk to some persons. So it is on that basis that we concluded that he was the person who talked -- who communicated between the inside of the camp and the leadership outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, "the leadership outside"?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, this can be inferred, or at least I can infer this; the KP Dom had a warden and its leadership, so to speak, but then the outside leadership of the SDS and the authorities in general would give them instructions as to what would be done. It is probably those who worked on this know this the best. We, the others, can only conclude this on the basis of events, of the events that we have seen. But it is not on the basis of some kind of internal organisation of theirs that we can infer this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have personal contacts with Mr. Todovic? Did you have conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, I didn't. Once, but I cannot say exactly whether it was he or Obrenovic that I talked to, or whether it was both of them or one of them only. I know that I was there, but it was something peripheral, some kind of information, but I can't remember now; something that is unimportant, since I haven't remembered it, registered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Todovic wearing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, he wore a military uniform, and from time to time, he wore a blue KP Dom uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "from time to time," does it mean during a certain period or did it change from day to day? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not from day to day. He didn't even come to the KP Dom any day -- every day. But from what I noticed, sometimes he wore a military uniform and sometimes he would wear the uniform that the KP Dom guards wore. That is from the civilian period of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Rasevic, what was he wearing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always wore the uniform that he wore before the war as well, as commander of the guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned this Mr. Gagovic. When did he come and what -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came sometime in July. I did not know him personally from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his position? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a deputy or perhaps he held the same function as Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I drew that conclusion from the fact that he toured guard posts, and also, when there were those roll calls in the evening, he would come, but he was not one of the guards who did shifts within the KP Dom. And I found out from the others that he also worked at the KP Dom in Zenica before the war as a kind of rehabilitation officer, so we came to the conclusion that he was at a higher level than others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that the guards were the former guards that worked there before the war. What did they wear when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all the staff that worked on internal security, except for persons who did not work in the KP Dom and who did work as guards inside, they all wore blue uniforms, the ones that they had worn before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were detained until the 4th of April, 1993. Can you tell us briefly -- not the details so much, the details. Can you briefly tell us how you could leave the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that exchanges were in groups, individual, or in smaller groups or individual. We did not know where and how people were taken away. It was a Sunday, the 4th of April. Around 2.00, according to the same procedure, a guard came to the door of our room, he opened the door, he called out my name, he said that I should get ready, I should take my belongings, and that I would be going for an exchange. I got ready and I waited in the room for about 45 minutes. Then those who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were my friends gave me addresses and messages for me to convey to their families once I was freed. Then the guard came and took me to the gate. Three men had already brought there from the isolation cell. We had never registered their existence. Probably they were brought in sometime during the night when we could not see. They were all unkempt. They had beards. I talked to them just a bit as we were waiting there to be searched. I asked them where they were from. They were three peasants from the village of Toholji. They were hiding, but then they were found by their homes. That's what they said. So when they searched all four of us and when they took some of the things that we had away from us, I had had some notes, something having to do with the German language. Everything that was in writing was taken away. In front of the gate of the KP Dom we had a vehicle waiting for us, a Russian-manufactured vehicle, GAZ, and there was a soldier there who took us over, Filipovic. I can't remember his first name. He was a waiter before the war. His nickname was Lovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... just the basic -- the most important facts.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that they took us to -- that he took us to town, and then very shortly he took me to Niksic under a false name. And in Niksic I found out that my family, my wife, in various conversations that took place before that, accepted to pay a certain amount of money for my release, and that I would be freed if a certain price was paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How high was the price?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out that they had asked for 100.000 Deutschemarks, but they bargained and finally agreed on 80.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were 80.000 Deutschemarks paid for you, for your release?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first 40.000 was paid, and then through the house that I had in Tivat, an additional 20, or rather, the entire house, so let's say all of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom was it paid? Who got the money, and where did this person get the money?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Mr. Filipovic said, the person who escorted me, there was some kind of agreement between the leadership, the military leadership in Foca, and also the leadership of the camp was supposed to be involved, too. Somebody who was meritorious. This was supposed to be divided among them. And the money was handed over as I crossed the border between Yugoslavia and Hungary at a duty-free shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who got the money? Who in person got the money; this Filipovic you mentioned or someone else?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was taken over by persons who were from Montenegro who were intermediaries, organisers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way, either in Foca or through Niksic and to the borders, was any -- did you meet any high-ranking military person? Would you know who was involved from the military leadership that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. But Filipovic himself who organised this, when he left the GAZ vehicle and the three peasants, he came with a white Golf to Foca with license plates that said the "Army of Republika Srpska." That's the kind of license plates that he had. And he took me out in this Golf, and then Tjentiste, Gacko, Bileca, we passed all of those under a false name. I had the identity card of a Serb, Ivanovic, and we pretended that I was a person who was wounded and was being taken to Igalo for recuperation. I don't know this man, and, of course, it would be strange for somebody to get into the KP Dom and to get somebody out of it without having received approval before that, somebody's permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What became of the other three peasants you mentioned that were taken out together with you, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Filipovic left me with Dragan Todovic in a private Muslim house until he returned, and this return took about an hour and a half or two, because when he left me there, then he took those three away. I don't know their names. I don't know what their fate was and whether these persons ever reappeared anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the document that is in the trial binders, ID 214. You can use this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at it, and this is a -- tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. We're getting no translation of any of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can, now. There's no answer at all. Do you need the answer to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. It was being interpreted while it was being given, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'd better ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what it is, this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document bears the date of the 21st of December, 1992, in its heading. It was obtained by my wife. She personally had requested it from the office of the International Red Cross in Zagreb. In this document, it says that I am in the camp, but that this is not on the basis of the records established by the Red Cross but on the basis of the records established by the local authorities. This is the provision of the local authorities. Later, in the Red Cross as I was trying to locate various persons, I realised that this provision was written for many persons, although they were missing. For example, for one of my wife's brothers, there's nothing, and in the case of another one of her brothers, it says that he was recorded by the local authorities. We imagined that several lists were made in the KP Dom on several occasions, and one of these lists reached the Red Cross, or only the list that the camp authorities or the Serb authorities in Foca submitted to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a date on this document saying a date of detention, 30 September 1992. Were you registered on that day by the Red Cross? Did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says here "local authorities." That's the only thing it says. As for the International Red Cross, in Zagreb I asked them why they did not -- I mean, they gave certificates to other persons that I mentioned, with their name, surname, and an internal number given to such persons by the International Red Cross, and the date when this person was registered as such. And other things are said only if somebody else had seen this person. So the assumption is that they got a document from the local authorities with the date of the 30th of September, 1992. That is the only explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the word "local authorities" -- the words "local authorities," are they the ones on the last line of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't have the document right now. I gave my version -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The Prosecution would like to enter this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be Exhibit P214.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, did you suffer any long-term physical or psychological consequences of your detention?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to the best of my ability to prevent any kind of adverse effects. While we were in camp, we had a group of doctors with us, and they kept telling us what this starvation can do to us. When I left the camp, I weighed about 57 or 58 kilograms. I had lost about 38 kilograms then. The doctors said that further exhaustion could lead to further atrophy of all the internal organs. There can be anorexia, and we might even pass away even without physical mistreatment. In Samobor, I received some medication and underwent this gradual recuperation. It was difficult for my organism to take all of this in, so my feet and legs would swell. As for the psychological consequences, a person remembers all of this every now and then. You try to suppress it, but then when you see the families of the persons who are no longer there, this keeps bringing it back to you, but I try to accept this so that there are no further consequences. But what else life has in store, that you never know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lojo.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney at law and one of the defence counsel for the accused Mr. Krnojelac. I will start with my questions from the very beginning, the beginning of your examination-in-chief yesterday. Yesterday you spoke of the Serb forces and Serb people, et cetera. What about the Muslim people in Foca, the Muslim entity in Foca; did they also have their armed units?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The form of organisation of the military part, we cannot say that it existed. There were legal institutions of the state, and I think that legal institutions are those that voted as they did in the referendum which was accepted by the Badinter commission; that is to say, that most citizens had opted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Until agreement was reached at the conference, I mean, there is the confusion between Serb forces of this kind and that kind. And whether on the Muslim side there were some forces, some people that were organised, there were some, but you cannot say that they were military formations. There was fear because Foca was in a specific position. There were threats from the Serb side. Because Foca was the host town of the founding assembly of the SDA, they said that Foca would have a price to pay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what you said. The congress when the SDA was established was held in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, well, I didn't mean the congress. I meant a rally that was held, a big rally in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people rallied together at this rally?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were about 100.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are both speaking over the translators. Please pause after the answer before you ask the question, Mr. Bakrac, and Mr. Lojo, would you please pause after the question before you start your answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I made a mistake for not having cautioned the witness about this, but I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Lojo, the fact that this meeting involving 100.000 persons in -- was held in Foca, that led to Muslims arming themselves? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't agree with any nationalist party that was established; I have to say that. So in that respect, I did not agree with this kind of rally or also the way in which it was prepared and the way it manifested itself. However, it was a pretext for certain Serb forces -- and you know that the rally was held, because in 1942, in Foca, a big crime was committed by the Chetnik forces when over two and a half thousand persons were killed. This kind of manifestation was not appropriate. But that is why there were threats that were issued. Then the SDA and the SDS were coalition partners, but in form rather than in substance. They took over. They took over power in Foca. And after this rally, a big rally of the SDS was held in Foca. So how should I put this? There was this potential conflict that was in the making between the two at the time. Just one more thing: In Cajnice, in 1991, on a big holiday, you can find it in the press also, Mr. Maksimovic said that Foca will either be Serb or it will be no more, and it was for these reasons why people began to feel fear, and events around the Focatrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You follow the press. Would you know from the press or from television that Senad Sahinpasic, called Saja said publicly, and wrote that, even before, a long time before the conflict broke out, he had been arming Muslims in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he wrote. And as for the statements that the arming was going on on the other side too, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does "the other side" mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say members SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, is it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, you also spoke about the SDS Crisis Staff. Did the SDA have its Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That form of organisation did not exist that I would call a Crisis Staff. I can't really speak with competence about certain things. From Taid Lojo, because I was not a member of the party, but he's a relative and he was municipal mayor, and I heard from him that the Muslim Bajram, which was the 3rd, 4th and the 5th, would be a bloody time for Muslims. And because of this situation, because in Foca was really the most typical of them all, he called various people, he called me, as the mine manager, "What do we do? How do we preserve peace after the first strike?" We believed profoundly, and I did, that the international community would prevent any large-scale conflict, because you must know that on the 6th of April, the European Community and the United States had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we thought that that recognition would help the reason to prevail, at least in the early days, to preserve peace, not to have any fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what you were saying. My question was whether there was a Crisis Staff, and you said that perhaps that was not how you would call it but a form of organisation?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Crisis Staff in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, I know it's hard but it's very difficult. You're making it almost impossible for the interpreters. Just wait until the question has been translated. You should be actually able to hear something in your earphones. Now you proceed with your answer. I'm sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise, but the communication -- so in the SDA, there was a form, I wouldn't call it a Crisis Staff, but the SDA had it, but to we who were executives there, without being a party leader, we would be called and our advice would be sought as to what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. You said yesterday that after a group of Serbs was killed, a PA system mounted on a car announced to the Muslims not to leave their homes. Doesn't it sound logical to you that what it meant was to protect them, was the protection of Muslims, to avoid any vengeance? How did you interpret this announcement after those Serbs were killed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, but I wouldn't interpret it as a result of their wish to protect us, although perhaps some may interpret it that way. I rather think that it was another form of repression, that those who were still there could possibly be resettled or perhaps brought into the camp, because there were murders of Muslims before that. Quite a number of members of well-known families there had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. You mentioned pressure to force the Muslims to move out. You already said here, and I do not think this is in dispute, that you already gave a statement to OTP investigators on the 25th and 26th of April, 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the one that the Prosecutor's office has here, because I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be of any help --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only gave one statement, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it help you if I showed you the statement? That is the statement that we were given by the OTP. And it has the signature and it says that this statement was read out to you in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of your knowledge and recollection. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that in that statement on page 3, you said the following: "On the 11th of April, 1992, the SDS gave an ultimatum -- submitted an ultimatum to the Muslims to hand over all the weapons. I learned that from Taid Lojo who told me about the ultimatum. After the ultimatum, many Muslims decided to flee Foca by whatever means available to them because SDA had said that the Muslims should leave during the night between the 14th and 15th April, 1992." Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just now you said that the Muslims left under pressure. Now we hear that you stated -- and you said that it is correct -- that it was the SDA which advised Muslims to leave Foca and that Muslims were leaving Foca.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me clarify it. Yes, I did say that. Because the SDS played a double role all the time. In the evening they were conducting negotiations about peace, and then they appointed a group, and I was also nominated for that group, the group to supervise the cease-fire. And meanwhile, new groups, new forces, were being brought in. And I must say that, at first instance, not even the Serb population, either the majority of them, did not favour war, because in those first two or three days, we jointly hid in cellars. But to encourage war and the conflict, they were looking for as conflicting situation as possible. They never complied with the cease-fire and they began to use the weapons - the SDS, I mean - without any cause or reason, and those weapons, rather shells, began to hit the areas where they were Muslim majorities. The SDS -- when I said ultimatum, the SDS requested that weapons be handed over without guaranteeing your life. And they had much stronger forces, especially with the help of the JNA troops, because there were armoured cars and vehicles. And the SDA -- when I say recommended, that is advised, because in Donje Polje, there were concentrations there, they recommended it because so as to avoid victims because the people panicked. They didn't know where to get away from those shells so as to move towards Ustikolina and further on, because there was a danger that these might enter and slaughter them all. Members of the White Eagles and others; in the early days Foca was full of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. Tell us also, are you aware that any of high-ranking SDA officials from Sarajevo issued such advice, such instructions, in other places to the Muslims, threatening even that those who didn't want to leave would have to do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, I'm going back to your statement that you made to OTP investigators, in which you said that you were first put in Room 16, and you repeated that in your testimony, and that you were also in Rooms 11 and 21. During the examination-in-chief, you never mentioned Room 11.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is an error. I do not think who wrote 11. I said 18. What the translator said I don't know, because 11 did not exist any longer -- I mean, there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. Yesterday with regard to poor diet, poor food in the KP Dom, you were asked by my learned friend and you said that you were sure it was a deliberate attempt on the part of the Serb authorities to starve you. In your notes that we saw here before the Court I found the following, and it was written by your hand: "The supply with foodstuffs is poor. The shops are not working, and one or two which do work have run out of supplies." I don't want to read it all, but that was within the context of the situation in Foca at the time of your detention.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. That is what I wrote. That was the situation in the town itself. That is not the situation in those parts which are controlled by the army, and the army controls the flour mill, the trading company. It controls all the warehouses in the town itself, and unfortunately that is how it was, even though apart from Donje Polje there was not much fighting. But the department store, and I said yesterday, and all the shops in the centre of the town were looted and ransacked by Serb military authorities. I saw it through the window. And those were not Focans, those were man who had come from Serbia. They were pulling out things from Maglic stores, and that is what I meant, that organisation of life in the town and life in the town was that way. Why it was, well, that is something that those who ran the town should know and those whom they had brought. So it was a situation, a desperate situation. But as for the food itself, they themselves had enough of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you properly, you said that the economic situation, and now you have told us, was intolerable. Now, you just said -- now, you spoke about the impossible situation, about a very bad situation. You were referring to the economic situation, weren't you? And you have to tell me, not to nod your head.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I will. I will tell you. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to end. I'm referring to the town itself, but I must mention, was that the -- was that how the Serb authorities treated their own people? I won't go into it. And that is what I meant. Because wheat from the flour mill, and I can confirm it, were taken by vehicles from Montenegro. Why they were depriving themselves of food, I do not know. But in Perucica, which was a trade company, it belonged to the military before the war, and they had large food reserves. What did they do with that? Did they feed the Serb people with that? I don't know. But as for the army and all the others, that was not the way to feed us, the way they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I understand your answer, you say that you were fed by the army in the camp?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the army, but the camp must have been under the patronage of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. Yesterday when you answered the questions asked of you by my learned friend, you said that in the camp, in the prison, there was one Alija you say from Gorazde, and I think you recalled his last name today, that he was called Alija Cardaklija, and that he complained of the conditions, that he sent these to the warden, and that two days later he was taken out and did not return. You also said that none -- that nobody else dared do something like that. In your statement to the OTP, you never once mention this person, Alija Cardaklija, nor that incident with his writing; but instead on page 4 of your statement, you wrote the following: "I talked to the superiors complaining of food and conditions. Perhaps it wasn't a wise thing to do, but I felt I could do that." Now is that correct, that you complained of the food and conditions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I spoke with Mr. Rasevic. I asked him, "Can something be done about the food?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen to you after that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why didn't you mention this incident with Alija Cardaklija? Why didn't you mention it to the OTP before today?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you can take it I couldn't really remember all the incidents at the time I gave my statements. It depended on questions that I was asked by investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us that you also spoke to journalists and that you assumed came from Serbia, and that you said how you were not soldiers, that one man came from the street, and so on and so forth. I won't repeat it. Could this be also interpreted as an objection to your detention?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could interpret it as an objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something untoward happen to you after that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you also said that your room was above a warehouse -- above the storage room. Which room did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that the Room 16 was above the makeshift storage room.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean there was a vehicle with the canvas raised, and through the window we could see foodstuffs loaded onto it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there wasn't a storage room, there was a vehicle below; do I understand you well? What kind of a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this food being loaded, unloaded, or just there in that truck?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was being unloaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it being taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the storage room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the storage room which was below your room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. I guess it was below my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But are you -- do you know that there was a storage room below Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you, or is it a guess?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have an opportunity to go out and check whether it was directly beneath my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went out for your meals, couldn't you see whether there was a storage room there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that distance, I couldn't really identify all the rooms, but on the front side -- it can be clarified if you have a sketch of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. You also said -- you also answered one of the questions in the examination-in-chief that one of the detainees who worked in the farm, that you were infested with lice from that person. Was something done in the KP Dom about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, the male nurse, Jokanovic, would enable us to come by powder against lice, and then we would use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the end of it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday and today you mentioned that some rooms -- or, rather, rooms in the ground floor of the administrative building were painted over. Was that also the case with windows of the prisoners' premises? Were they closed in some way?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The detainees' windows were not painted over, and they were of transparent glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you also said that, perhaps in not so many words, but throughout your stay in the KP Dom you never saw anyone beat anyone except for that one incident, nor did you see anyone killed in the KP Dom? I say "see."

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly to have seen somebody being beaten or killed, no, except ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct -- is it correct that you said that detainees in upper rooms could hear objects being thrown into the Drina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some comments in the morning in passing, that those people would say how they had heard some splash against the water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those were the comments?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also page 5 of your statement, you say that you heard about corpses which float down the river to Gorazde. During -- who controlled Gorazde during the conflict? Who had the power in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of BiH army held Gorazde, and it was on the radio. On the transistor I heard Radio Sarajevo, and from time to time they gave the names of persons who had been pulled out of the Drina arriving from the direction of Foca, Josanica, and downstream towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, throughout the war, Gorazde was downstream, and it was held by Muslims, and they pulled out those bodies which floated down the Drina, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all along the stream -- the course of the Drina because from Josanica -- Ustikolina to Josanica, it was all held by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And downstream, then, it was Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Josanica to Gorazde, yes, but the bodies were flowing from the direction which was controlled by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn if any of those persons was perhaps found in the Drina or taken out of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about them, but I heard about another person whose personal papers had been found and who came from Miljevina. It was one of my workers who had been taken and allegedly returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find that person at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that that group, which might include that person whom you mentioned, could have been taken from the KP Dom to Miljevina and did not come back to the KP Dom? Do you mean that group?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, may I repeat a question, because the transcript says that nobody was found of those persons, and my question was about persons who were taken from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as to make it clear, did you also understand that I meant those persons, and that your answer referred to those persons who had been taken from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you also spoke about another incident when three Cengices were taken away from the KP Dom, or rather, released from the KP Dom. Is it correct that you said the following: "On the day of their release, an army -- high-ranking army officer, Kovacevic or Bozevic, I don't know the first name, ordered the guard to bring out those three."

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Presumably it must have come down the chain of command. It couldn't have been done directly. That is what the persons said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, when you say that is what that person said, you mean whom? Cengices?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Cengices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page in that same statement, you said the following: "The KP Dom guards could not and did not prevent the soldiers from entering the KP Dom. We lived in fear and suspense. Before I was brought to the KP Dom, there was a group of Serb guards who played the part of guards awaiting for reassignment." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two or three days while I was there, there were a few soldiers, members of the Serb forces from Serbia. And according to what the detainees who had arrived there before me, they said that in the camp there were a number of soldiers from Serbia who were accommodated there and performed, because at that time before the camp was organised by former members of the KP Dom who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Lojo. Your Honours, perhaps this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, before the break, we talked about the guards at the KP Dom. Today, during the examination-in-chief, you said that the guards, those who worked in the KP Dom previously, wore blue uniforms that were worn at the KP Dom before the outbreak of the war conflict as well. Other guards who had not worked in the KP Dom before that, did they wear uniforms too?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wore military uniforms but sometimes the other ones who wore blue uniforms also wore camouflage uniforms, but that was more seldom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to us just now that those who worked in the KP Dom earlier on, who wore blue uniforms, sometimes wore camouflage uniforms as well. What about the guards who worked at the KP Dom? Did they take breaks, and during those breaks, did they go to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, there were some who went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During the examination-in-chief and also in response to my question, you spoke about the pressure exerted upon Muslims to leave Foca, and yesterday you also mentioned some other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Today I asked you about your statement in which you said that the SDA had given an instruction to leave Foca, that Muslims were supposed to leave Foca. Do you know the name Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name Hasan Cengic. Except I have to correct you. It was not an instruction; it was a sort of call. There was nothing in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a call that was addressed orally to the Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there was an attack at Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you know the name Hasan Cengic. Who is this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the secretary of the SDA of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to read a document to you, to show you a document, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I did this at a late stage. Before we resumed, I gave copies to the interpreters so that they could follow this more easily but I'm going to read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note they do not have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreters say that they do not have the copies. Who did you give it to for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave it to the registrar, but late, late, lest there be any misunderstanding. I think that the mistake is mine. I gave it to her just before we resumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just wait a moment so that it can be sent into the interpreters. Right. You proceed now, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that was written on letterhead of the Party of Democratic Action. It was addressed to the SDA Trebinje, and it is entitled, "Instruction concerning moving out of Trebinje." "Since the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina is becoming increasingly complex from the point of view of security, especially after the Geneva documents were accepted by Karadzic and his clique at Pale, it is necessary, with a view to the implementation of the aspirations of all Muslims, the preservation and strengthening of our state, Bosnia and Herzegovina, to urgently take the following measures in the area of the Trebinje municipality. "Number 1: Through our activists, all Muslims should be encouraged to leave Trebinje and go to Montenegro, especially prominent and well-to-do citizens. "Property moveable and immovable should be sold in part, and if possible, it should be left in the care of Serbs that enjoy confidence and that Muslim friends know from beforehand who are opponents of Karadzic's renegade policies. "Number 3, not to hesitate to exert pressure and even force against those Muslims who do not act in accordance with this order. Upon arriving in Montenegro, linkup with the SDA, Merhamet and our people in the Liberal Federation of Montenegro where you will receive all instructions in terms of further action. Every religious facility of ours in Montenegro shall render assistance to you, and our brothers in Tuzi, Podgorica, Plav, and Rozaje, and throughout Montenegro await you. "Number 5, all of your property will be compensated for when we attain our objective, and we will know how to appreciate your sacrifice, and this is what the Muslims of the world expect of you. With respect, Salem Olejkum [phoen], the secretary of the SDA, Hasan Cengic". The instruction that we discussed, the one that was given to Muslims in Foca, was it given in this respect, in this sense, like what I just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this sense. I don't think that this one is authentic either because its date is controversial. As far as I know, Trebinje was abandoned in June and July 1992, so I find this instruction quite questionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a certain number of Muslims from Foca go to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the only way one could leave Foca. Either when people were leaving individually in April and May, or later when it was organised by the Serb authorities, as my wife and children left later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see a signature here and a stamp, a seal of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to make any comments. I was just wondering about the date, the 20th of January, 1993. It seems quite pointless, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your assertion that -- is it your assertion that on the 21st of January, 1993, there were no Muslims in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what your assertion is?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of individuals, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lojo, I shall continue my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you do, the booth up there had better try Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do something about the speakers, which are crackling quite loudly all the time. Thank you. You proceed, thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However I -- oh, yes, now I can -- now I do have the right kind of sound in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you talked about persons who went to work, and in your statement you said that the persons who were in charge of the KP Dom asked for volunteers to go out to work, and they were privileged in some way and you explained that. You said that also a workroom was composed in this way, that is to say, of such persons. Which room was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Room 16, after the 31st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 31st of October, 1992, was there some kind of a working room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Room 19, as far as I can remember, but then my memory fails me a bit now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this room, number 16, after October 1992 -- or from October 1992 onwards was the workroom. Was it the workroom until the last day of your stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that in the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said on page 7 that after the Red Cross entered the KP Dom in June 1993, the food became better and there was more freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, having heard about it from the people I saw later when they got out as well, in 1994, 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to ask, how come you knew about that. Tell me another thing: Did the Red Cross enter the KP Dom before that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- for as long as I was there, no, not while I was there. However, before I was brought in, other inmates say that the Red Cross did enter briefly, or rather, a lady who we could identify as the person who transferred two or three wounded persons from the hospital to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lojo, when you told the investigators of the OTP about your release, is it true that you said the following? There's no need for me to read to you what you confirmed as something that you know. "Filipovic, whose name I do not know, a soldier who was a member of some kind of special unit, awaited me outside. I did not notice that on that occasion some other person who was in charge of the KP Dom was present or participated in my release." Is it correct that you stated that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I stated that, that there was no one there except for the cook and the guard in front of the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that no one else out of the persons in charge of the KP Dom was present or took part in your release?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Took part? I mean specifically that day, that's probably what I had in mind. I don't even know who did take part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who took part. Today you said that it was those who were running the KP Dom in Foca who were also supposed to get their share of the money received. On which basis are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what Mr. Filipovic said who escorted me. He said that in the organisation of the command in Foca, and now I'm adding the following, that somebody had to issue orders to the people at the KP Dom as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Filipovic said to you only that you were released through the organisation of the command in Foca, and the rest is your assumption; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that as far as the abuse of Mandzo and Dzanko was concerned, that they were beaten by a certain Ivanovic, their neighbour, who was not a guard at the KP Dom. Do you know the name of Risto Ivanovic, a guard at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he treat persons of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Risto Ivanovic is concerned, I stated, as probably the others did as well, that he was very decent, that he was a man who was prepared to help and -- although his brother was killed, that is to say a member of his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is not the Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was not a guard and that he beat these persons with a rifle butt. Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was because this was outside the compound. However, the fact is that he did this in the KP Dom in cooperation with the guards who came in and who took these persons out. Why it was that way, we really do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this incident, you also said that, opposed to other incidents that occurred during the night - if I remember correctly, you said between 1700 and 2100 hours - this happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a working day or it was a Saturday or a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Saturday, but I don't know whether it was a workday or not. I don't know about the organisation of work at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While you stayed at the camp, did you have the possibility of following press, radio? Did you obtain any kind of information?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of this was made possible to us, nor did we know what was happening. Only I, from time to time, while I had a transistor which had been taken in surreptitiously before that, we listened to it until, say, August, 1992, until the guards took it away from me and we were deprived of all the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it via that radio that you heard about the London conference?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you talked about Radojica Tesovic, the previous warden. Do you know that for some time in the month of April, that person was absent from Foca? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to information received from persons who were with Mr. Tesovic, just when the fighting started, that is to say shooting in Foca, on the 8th and 9th, Mr. Tesovic and Milutin Tijanic organised the transfer of the then prisoners via Velecevo, the female prison, towards Montenegro. Part of them allegedly left the camp and they were seen at Velecevo, and they spent the entire month there at Velecevo. Selimovic Ekrem and Selimovic Sead talked to them. This was in mid-April; I mean the 8th, 9th, 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did they stay in Montenegro and Serbia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything else about their movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, today you talked about the Territorial Defence and the reserve forces, military reserve forces. Were you there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I did my service in the JNA, I was not on the reserve force. For a brief period of time, I was on the reserve force of the state security, and since later I became the holder of a high office, that is to say I was party secretary and then director of the mine, et cetera, so I was not part of the active force, either of the JNA or of the Territorial Defence, but I held the office in accordance to which office I held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other citizens of Foca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have been doing this most of the time. You've got to give that pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't hear an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was speaking to Mr. Bakrac. He keeps on asking his question whilst we are still getting the translation of the answer. So please, Mr. Bakrac, just pause. Have you not got the translation running in your ears?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I hear you and I try to hear what you're saying in English. I understood what you said. However, there seemed to be interruptions in my headphones, also in the witness's headphones, judging by what he's just said. It comes and goes intermittently, the interpretation we are supposed to receive. Your Honour, perhaps that is the reason why, when there is this interruption, I think that the interpretation is over and then I speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we will see what can be done about the channel that you're listening on, but you usually go straight in when he was finished speaking, and you must know that the translation is still going. It is making it very difficult for the interpreters. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to use the transcription.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to intervene. I have not received a word of interpretation concerning everything that's been said, and I think it has something to do with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, since we are speaking the same language, I'll try to explain it to you. It was my mistake, Mr. Lojo. We speak the same language, so it is necessary for us to pause between our questions and answers because there needs to be interpretation of everything that we are saying. So that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just check the channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am on channel 6, but I haven't translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will see what we can do, whether there is some fault with channel 6, because both sides seem to be complaining about it. If you're worried about channel 6, I am listening on channel 6 and I can't hear anything either.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can the interpreters speak something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it's more important that we have somebody from the translation booth giving us something on channel 6, and then we will see whether we can hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, one, two, three. Can you hear the English booth?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, English booth is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think help is on the way.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the technician is on his way to the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I've just picked up something on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's see how we go, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, did other people from Foca, regardless of their ethnic origin, were they members of the reserve force of the Territorial Defence, regardless of whether they had served in the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose according to the combat orders, they were either in the JNA reserve force or with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the same rule apply to them, up to what age they had, they were under this obligation?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to all of the citizens, to all the citizens, all the nationals, of the former Yugoslavia, that is Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, how frequently were military drills held?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the programme. It was once or twice a year usually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the war conflict broke out, when was the last military drill, do you know? In the area of Foca, of course.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I was more conversant with it while I was the mayor of the municipality or, rather, the secretary of the committee, because ex officio I had then, of course, to keep abreast of such things. When I became the manager of the mine, I didn't know any more about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember some drill after 1986?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there was. There must have been also in 1987 and 1988 and 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. Did you, in your notes, mention the victimisation of Serbs in a place called Josanica?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened and when did it happen; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we did not know, but when it came out I learnt about it. However, we supposed that it was on Saint Nikolas's day, that is, on the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what year? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. Because in terms of shelling from rocket mortars ensued from the town towards -- in the direction of Gorazde, and there were alarms and we could hear things around the town, that something was underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then learn what happened?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learned, from the direction of Gorazde a unit, a military formation, I don't know how many and who, made an inroad, an incursion in the village of Josanica which is below the hospital, and on that occasion they killed quite a number, that is, over 70 men, women, children, and civilians -- that is, all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lojo. My learned friend went with you through the list that you had compiled. At that time when you were doing that, did you at the same time communicate with the Red Cross and look at the information they had in their computer?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I compiled this list before the Red Cross. You can see my handwriting. And there are some names missing from it because I simply could not remember them at the time. And then after I communicated with the Red Cross, I saw some other names -- I mean, I knew people, but I didn't know that those were their names, and I saw them in the -- at the International Red Cross in the Zagreb office computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this, you made the second list which you wrote in capital letters?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you made this other list in capital letters?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend went through it date by date and your information; however, the Defence is unclear, and I should like to invite you to clarify it. With regard to the exchange on the 29th of August, 1992, you also indicated that it was Saturday, in the afternoon hours, and there was a group of 71 prisoners. I was writing down very carefully where you had your contacts, but you gave three names for this group. Hasan Dzano, did you communicate with one of his relatives, with a member of his family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after I came out. His wife, as far as I know, committed suicide. I don't know about other members of his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you communicate with some members of Emir Mandzo's family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with his wife who was in Skopje because my wife's parents were also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it that you communicated with her?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Sanin Kulelija from Visegrad, did you communicate with a member of family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from his family, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are only three names out of 71, and you say -- stated, and said it again today, that the others never called anyone. Could you give us the names of those 71, and with whose families did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of these 71, it was very intensive from all rooms. I suppose with some family or other, but I never tried again to reconstruct the name of those people because I assumed that other witnesses also knew some of them. I didn't go out to try to research on all 400 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you can reconstruct only these three persons from the list?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you explain to us how you communicated with them and why. Also in the view of the Defence, the exchange of September 10, 1992, also raises some questions. You tell us that 41 prisoners were taken away on that occasion, but here you gave only six names. Fadil Divjan, did you communicate with any members of his family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did in Germany where there was somebody of his next of kin when I was there in 1993 in Munich, a place near Munich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think but you're not sure about that April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, because the fact is that none of them ever called to let anybody know they were alive. I think I would be very happy to learn that one -- some of them are still among the living, but so far none of them have communicated with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lojo, I fully agree with you, but our task here is to establish certain facts and evidence, and my question specifically was, are you sure that you communicated with somebody, some member of his family, or aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer because I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Edhem Kafedzic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have, same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meho Hadzimesic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same again, because they all come from Slatina, and I therefore did not know their next of kin. They did not come from Foca, from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Semso Cankusic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same then holds true of Reko and Rahman, is it; same thing, same case?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the only questionable thing is the exchange on the 12th of September, 1992, when you said that there was a group of 50 prisoners, yet you mention only four names. So my question is the same as in the previous case: Who did you communicate with and did you? Fehim Isanovic, did you speak to anyone, to any member of his family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that group of those who killed or not? I didn't have a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it depends on it. You should know whether you communicated with somebody from Fehim Isanovic's family. Why do you need to look which group they belong to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except Mezbur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, only with Mezbur's family; and with Sefko Hodzic's family and Hidajet Srna's family you did not communicate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we have the witness's answer repeated, please? The interpreters didn't hear it. The question was you only checked with Mezbur's family, and with Hodzic's family and Hidajet Srna's family you did not communicate with. Do you remember what answer you gave to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. I said it was the same thing as before. The only family I communicated with was Mezbur's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not communicate with these other families?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your list, sir, you list 17 names, and you say they were taken out in the afternoon and did not come back; and I want to ask you to tell us to the best of your recollection, what rooms were they taken from? Munib Veiz, what room was he taken from and when? No, excuse me, you did say 15th to the 30th, you could not say the date. But what room was he taken away from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I can now get the exact numbers of those rooms, because it was only a short time after we were brought to the camp, within the 20 days. But they were taken out from rooms, by and large, number 13, 15, and 14, as far as I can remember, by and large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Room 14 was -- had the same entrance as you, you shared the entrance, didn't you, into the building with Room 14?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it shouldn't be. Sixteen is the first number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kruno Marinovic, what room was he taken from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mato Ivancic, what room was he taken from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, this is too -- it was too early for me to know these things. All I know is that I saw them at the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you mention that he was taken from Room 21?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Room 21 when I arrived, I found his passport there. I don't know that he himself was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Room 21 you found his documents?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But how they got there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Room 13 or maybe 15, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mirko Niksic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Room 13, perhaps Room 15, that is ground floor or the room above it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Selimovic called Spona?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, none of them were in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zulfo Veiz in a room which shared your entrance?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fuad Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, same entrance. Whether Room 18 or perhaps one above, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your entrance, that is in the right wing of the prisoners' quarters as you face them, is it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO [Resumed]
